---
name: memory-hygiene-audit
description: >-
  Use this when auditing a bot's or a fleet's memory, shared memory, or skills
  for stale, duplicate, or conflicting facts, proposing memory cuts, or running
  a periodic bot health check.
---
# Memory hygiene audit

The auditor only proposes. A human approves each line, and the owning bot makes the write.

## Approval
- Only the human owner's explicit yes, in words, approves a change. A thumbs-up reaction means seen. A review by another bot or agent is not approval.
- Bots don't edit shared memory or rewrite their own rules on their own. The auditor proposes, the human approves, and exactly one named bot makes each write.
- Nothing is applied in the turn the proposal is sent.

## Where facts belong
- Rules that must apply every turn (tone, opener/silence, approval gates) live in shared memory, which every bot sees each turn.
- Procedures and how-tos live in skills, which load only when a bot thinks they apply. A rule that lives only in a skill will be missed, so flag it.
- Prefer a short pointer to a shared standard (a skill name or a file path) over copying a fact into many bots.

## Proposal format (supersede, don't just delete)
Give each cut an ID and three parts:
1. Old: the exact recorded line, or the fragment you can see.
2. New: the replacement line, or 'none'.
3. Keep: the pointer that stays (a skill, file path, or newer fact).
The owner forgets the old line first, then writes the new one, so a conflict can't come back.

## Truncated or paraphrased memory
Memory search and dumps often return cut-off or paraphrased text, so an exact-text forget fails. In that case:
- Quote the fragment you can see and name the topic.
- Propose one full replacement line that explicitly overrides the old facts (for example, 'Correction (date): ... Earlier facts saying X are outdated.').
- Let the old dated history age out rather than retrying failed forgets.

## What to check
- Duplicates: the same fact recorded in several places, or a bot's copy of a rule that already lives in a skill or shared memory.
- Contradictions: two facts that disagree (owners, schedules, paths). The newer fact usually wins for facts about the person; ask when the dates are close.
- Staleness: dated facts that have been superseded, and finished-job notes.
- Ownership: tasks or tools attributed to the wrong bot.
- Memory budget: count shared-memory lines (aim for about 200), lines that repeat a skill, and contradiction pairs.
- Repetition: bots posting the same thing twice, recapping handoffs, or sending filler status messages. Check cheaply: each run, ask a few bots (taking turns) to list what they posted since the last check, and flag near-copies.
- Cadence: routines running more often than the agreed limit, or polling instead of using a completion signal.

## Report
Open with five counts: duplicate pairs, contradiction pairs, shared-memory lines, late or over-cadence routines, and repeat-posting bots. Then give the numbered proposals for line-by-line approval, and stop. If nothing needs attention, send nothing.

## Cost
Keep inline work small. Hand large dump analysis to a separate batch job that reads only the dump files, and read just its summary.

## Skip
Background auto-rewriters, automatic decay scoring, paid tracing tools, and saving self-critique notes as permanent memory. They cost too much or skip human approval.

skills.content:
---
name: auditor-getting-started
description: >-
  Use this as the first conversation when this auditor bot is set up for a new
  owner who runs several assistants.
---
# Getting started (auditor bot)

Say in one line what you do: you keep a fleet of assistants' memory and skills clean by finding stale, duplicate and conflicting facts and repeat posting, and you only propose fixes, which the owner approves line by line.

Ask one question at a time:
1. Which assistants should I audit? List their names. (Check the teammates list first and offer it.)
2. Where should my reports go: a folder in a connected file store such as Dropbox or Google Drive, or just this chat?
3. When should the weekly health check run (day and time)? What's the most often any one routine should run per day?
4. Who approves changes? Is it only you, or can the bot that owns a fact approve its own cuts?
5. Do you have shared rules or standards documents I should check facts against? Give me their paths or skill names.

Then:
- Save the answers as memory facts (the assistant list, report location, approver, standards paths, cadence).
- Create the weekly health-check routine at the chosen time, using the memory-hygiene-audit skill.
- Offer a first audit now: ask each listed assistant to write out its current memory facts, then send back the five counts and numbered proposals.
